oneLineAnswer: A strong prescription opioid, available as tablets, liquid or injections, for severe pain other medicines have not controlled.
whatItIs: Hydromorphone is a prescription opioid, a medicine that attaches to opioid receptors in the body. A receptor is a docking point on a cell that a chemical can switch on. The drug label describes it as a hydrogenated ketone of morphine, which means it is a modified form of morphine. The United States approved it in 1984. It is a controlled medicine, and labels sold in the United States mark it CII. Labels warn that it can be abused and misused, which can lead to overdose and death.
whatItDoes: It eases pain by switching on opioid receptors, mainly the mu-opioid receptor.
Doctors call it a full opioid agonist, which means it fully activates those receptors.
The label says its main therapeutic action is analgesia, the relief of pain.
It is meant only for pain severe enough to need an opioid.
howPeopleUseIt: Doctors prescribe it when pain is severe enough to need an opioid and other treatments have not worked or were not tolerated.
It comes as tablets and as an oral liquid that you swallow.
Hospitals also give it as an injection into a vein, a muscle, or under the skin.
The label notes that many acute pain conditions need no more than a few days of an opioid.
Studies in the public trial registry have tested it for pain after heart surgery and chest surgery.

commonSideEffects: The label lists lightheadedness, dizziness, sedation, nausea, vomiting, sweating, flushing, dry mouth, and itching as the most common effects.
Euphoria and dysphoria, a low or uneasy mood, are also listed.
Less frequent effects include constipation, headache, blurred or double vision, and trouble passing urine.
The medication guide tells patients about constipation, nausea, sleepiness, vomiting, tiredness, headache, dizziness, and belly pain.
seriousSigns: Slow or shallow breathing is the main danger; the label calls this respiratory depression.
The label lists respiratory arrest, circulatory depression, shock, and cardiac arrest as serious reactions.
Combining it with alcohol, benzodiazepines, or other depressants can cause deep sedation, coma, and death.
A medication guide flags trouble breathing, chest pain, and swelling of the face, tongue, or throat.
Serotonin syndrome, a serious reaction, has been reported when opioids are taken with other serotonin-raising drugs.
Adrenal insufficiency and severe allergic reactions called anaphylaxis have been reported after the drug reached the market.
Long-term opioid use has been linked to lower sex hormones and to increased pain sensitivity (hyperalgesia).
whoShouldAvoid: People whose breathing is already seriously slowed.
People with acute or severe asthma that is not being monitored or lacks resuscitation equipment.
Anyone with a known or suspected bowel blockage, including paralytic ileus.
Anyone allergic to hydromorphone or to medicines that contain sulfites.
People taking an MAOI antidepressant, or who stopped one in the past 14 days.
Older adults, who may be more sensitive to the drug.
People with liver or kidney problems, whose bodies handle the drug differently.
Children, because the safety and effectiveness have not been established.

interactions: Alcohol, benzodiazepines, and other central nervous system depressants: risk of profound sedation, breathing problems, coma, and death.
Serotonergic drugs, including some antidepressants: serotonin syndrome has been reported with combined use.
MAOIs, such as phenelzine, tranylcypromine, and linezolid: combined use is not recommended.
Mixed agonist or partial agonist opioids, such as buprenorphine, nalbuphine, pentazocine, and butorphanol: these may blunt the pain relief or trigger withdrawal.
Muscle relaxants: hydromorphone can add to their effect and increase breathing depression.
Diuretics: opioids can make these medicines work less well.
Anticholinergic drugs: combined use may raise the risk of urine retention and severe constipation.
Prescription or over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements can also interact, so the medication guide asks patients to tell their provider about all of them.
pregnancyAndChildren: The label says there are no available human data on whether hydromorphone raises the chance of major birth defects or miscarriage. Animal studies at high doses did show harm, and the label advises pregnant women about a possible risk to the fetus. Long use during pregnancy can cause withdrawal symptoms in a newborn, a condition that can be life-threatening if it is not recognized and treated. Some hydromorphone passes into breast milk, and the label says to watch a breastfed baby for extra sleepiness and slow breathing. Opioids used for a long time may lower fertility in women and men, and it is unknown whether that reverses. Safety and effectiveness in children have not been established.
whatWeDoNotKnow: No human studies show whether hydromorphone raises the risk of birth defects or miscarriage.
Safety and effectiveness in children have not been established.
It is not known whether opioid-related fertility problems go away after the medicine is stopped.
The label warns that side-effect rates from one trial cannot be compared with rates for another drug, so the true rates for hydromorphone are uncertain.
The sources fetched for this record contain no head-to-head test of hydromorphone against other opioids for safety.
The label does not describe long-term outcomes for people who take it for months or years.

summary: This record covers what hydromorphone is, how it is used for severe pain, its common and serious side effects, who should avoid it, its main interactions, and open questions, drawn from United States drug labeling and public health sources.
